transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-21
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Khan (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Maya Lin (Velociti), Rajesh Patel (Velociti SRE), Olivia Grant (Velociti Head of AI)

Summary: quick POC check-in to review recent TTFT regressions during streaming tests, decide quantization tradeoffs, and align on next steps for reproducing microbursts in Velociti's staging traffic. Some noise on call; a few names were mis-transcribed.

Topics: TTFT anomalies, streaming handshake vs buffered responses, sequence-length distribution, 4-bit quant impact, kernel fallback policy, replay plan for microburst repro.

[00:00] Aisha: okay, thanks everyone for joining, uh this is the weekly POC sync for Velociti. We wanted to go over the TTFT numbers from the ramp last night, and then pick a quant path. Diego is on deck for the perf slides.
[00:22] Diego: hey hi team, quick note — I uploaded the run logs to the shared drive, file microburst-20260520.tar.gz, link in the chat. The key thing we saw was a spike at t equals ~18 minutes where TTFT jumped from ~70ms to 350ms for a subset of requests.
[00:40] Maya: yeah that matches what we saw, we had a short flood from our analytics endpoint hitting longer prompts with seqlen ~640 to 800, and our staging routing kept them on the same pod.
[01:05] Rajesh: to clarify, the traffic shape was a batch of concurrent small streams, not single heavy threads, right?
[01:15] Maya: correct, multiple concurrent small streams and a couple long completions.
[01:28] Diego: what we think happened — and this is preliminary — is the KV cache plus sequence-length expansion pushed the kernel into a different execution path. On one GPU kernel the attention matmul fallback was less optimized for seqlen>512 and streaming buffer growth caused more copies.
[01:56] Olivia: sorry just to check, is this more likely a model kernel decision or an orchestration/batching mis-configuration?
[02:08] Diego: both. There's a kernel-level perf cliff for specific layer sizes; also the serving runtime's dynamic batcher picked a bundle that increased prefill overhead. We saw more prefix caching churn which increases TTFT.
[02:27] Aisha: and just to be clear, this was on Redwood Dedicated capacity right? The staging cluster that Velociti gave us — I think it was the dedicated pool with the q4_0 profile?
[02:40] Maya: yes dedicated pool, q4_0 quant. But our initial non-quant runs on hosted gave different shapes. Some of the proper nouns in the logs came out as 'Readwood' in the auto transcribe — ignore that.
[03:05] Diego: for next steps we recommended two parallel experiments: 1) reproduce microburst with traffic replay at seqlen buckets 128/256/512/768, 2) run quantization sweep 8-bit vs 4-bit for TTFT and output-quality on a small eval set.
[03:26] Rajesh: we can do the replay, but need a small script to throttle concurrency to match production-ish bursts. I'll own that.
[03:35] Maya: thanks. Also one wrinkle — our compliance team wants to keep the logs in-house, so Diego if you need logs you have to pull via the signed S3 link we shared earlier.
[03:48] Diego: that's fine, we've got the link.
[04:01] Olivia: can you remind us what the TTFT SLO we were aiming for again? I thought we had 100ms median and 150ms p95?
[04:12] Aisha: we had discussed 100ms median; Diego suggested p95 target of 120ms for typical routes. But for long streams we agreed to set realistic per-route SLOs; let's re-confirm in the follow-up.
[04:30] Diego: jumping into numbers — I pulled the kernel-level timeline. At the spike we saw an extra 220ms in the input prefill and KV cache stash. The actual decode path wasn't the primary culprit.
[04:50] Rajesh: is that because of extra memcpy or because kernel selection used a less optimal matmul?
[04:59] Diego: both — memcpy from the streaming layer plus a kernel pick that goes to 'generic-attn' instead of 'fast-attn' for seqlen>512 when residual buffer crosses threshold. We can try changing the kernel selection heuristic to favor fast-attn earlier but need to validate numerical stability.
[05:25] Maya: what about explicit seqlen bucketing at the routing layer? If we route seqlen>512 to a variant optimized for long sequences maybe we avoid the cliff.
[05:35] Diego: yes that's an option. Two model variants or compile profiles: one optimized for short streaming and another for long sequences. Redwood runtime supports routing by policy, we can configure a per-route compilation preference.
[05:50] Olivia: but that increases cost if we keep two pools warm, no?
[05:57] Aisha: yes there is a cost tradeoff. We can do canary routing first — only route a small percent of long requests to the long-optim profile and measure. Or we can use autoscale burst to handle the occasional long sequences.
[06:15] Rajesh: cost is a factor but reliability is more pressing for the analytics use-case. If a small percent of requests degrade user experience it's amplified.
[06:30] Diego: quant comes into play — in q4_0 we see lower memory footprint so more KV cache fits in GPU, which helps latency, but q4 reduces numerical headroom and sometimes causes tokenization differences that slow downstream post-processing.
[06:48] Maya: have you observed any hallucination or quality drop with q4 in previous pilots?
[06:55] Diego: small, on edge cases. Our plan is to run an automatic eval set of 500 prompts and also do a human spot-check for the top 50 long prompts.
[07:10] Olivia: and 4-bit vs 8-bit — what's the TTFT delta we should expect?
[07:16] Diego: from our internal numbers, 4-bit can give 10–20% TTFT improvement in steady-state for batchy workloads, but microburst sensitivity varies. It compacts KV cache so sometimes p95 improves more than median.
[07:33] Maya: okay — so action items: Diego runs the quant sweep; Rajesh builds the replay throttle; Aisha bundles the kernel matrix and the step-by-step how-to for routing rules.
[07:46] Diego: one more note — streaming handshake latency matters: if the RT pipeline waits for the full prefill rather than sending token 1 asap, TTFT is worse. We observed a variance in first token emission due to small timing differences in our streaming buffer flush policy.
[08:05] Rajesh: that sounds like a config change, not a kernel issue. Can you point to where that setting lives?
[08:12] Diego: it's in the runtime config under stream.flush.threshold and stream.prefill.strategy. We can test a 'first-token-buffer-size=1' to force early emission but need to see impact on bandwidth.
[08:30] Olivia: bandwidth vs TTFT — another cost tradeoff. If we flush earlier we might increase token overhead for small responses.
[08:40] Aisha: agreed. For the pilot we should aim for TTFT:90–120ms p95 for our key routes. We should measure bandwidth delta separately.
[08:52] Maya: also the SE noted a small regression when we enabled model-level kernel hedging; older kernels timed out and retried causing a cascade. Diego, did you see retrials in the logs?
[09:04] Diego: yes two retries showing in the tail logs — those retrials align with garbage-collected KV entries, the hedging caused a mismatch and we fell back to a slower path. We can tighten the hedging window or disable it for the short-ttl caches.
[09:25] Rajesh: better to disable hedging until we stabilize. Hedging is great for tail but it mixes kernels mid-request which seems unsafe for streaming.
[09:36] Diego: agreed — toggling hedging off for streaming routes is a safe default.
[09:45] Aisha: okay listing decisions so far: disable hedging for streaming routes, run quant sweep, prepare seqlen routing configs, and reproduce microburst via replay.
[10:00] Olivia: on security — we need to confirm that the signed S3 link approach meets our data residency rules, and the audit logs for the dedicated pool were requested by our compliance. Aisha, Diego, can you attach the audit-log examples?
[10:12] Aisha: yes I'll include a snippet. Diego will redact PII before sharing.
[10:18] Diego: noted, I'll sanitize and share.
[10:24] Maya: one practical ask — can Redwood provide a small script to toggle the kernel preference heuristics for a single pod? We want to run an A/B within our staging cluster.
[10:33] Diego: yes we can provide a one-line flag for the runtime agent or a config map example. I'll put that in the repo.
[10:40] Rajesh: perfect. Also I'll capture CPU side metrics and pod-level memory graphs for the next sync — might help isolate memcpy hotspots.
[10:50] Aisha: great.
[11:00] [Long middle section of detailed numbering, timestamps every minute as Diego walks through a few sample log lines — transcription gets a couple names wrong like 'Velocity' or 'Readwood' — omitting full raw logs here, refer to shared artifact link]
[33:12] Diego: quick callout from the quant run — the 4-bit run had one interesting case where p95 improved by ~40ms on seqlen 128 but at seqlen 768 we saw no improvement and occasionally a small degradation. We're likely hitting a path where more attention output alignment cost outweighs memory wins.
[34:05] Maya: that seems to indicate we should not blanket-deploy q4 for all routes. Instead pick seqlen and route buckets.
[34:22] Aisha: yes, rule-based routing by sequence length seems the least risky. Also we can keep an A/B with 5% of traffic to monitor quality metrics.
[35:03] Rajesh: about the replay — I'll try to reproduce the spike locally tonight with our script. If reproducible we can coordinate a live debug with Diego on Friday.
[35:20] Diego: Friday is fine, I'm free in the morning.
[35:30] Olivia: please add the compliance review to the calendar invite as an aside; I'll schedule a 30-min slot with our security lead next week.
[35:40] Aisha: will do.
[36:05] Diego: another subtle perf signal — garbage collection of small tensors during the streaming session caused short stalls around 200–300ms; we can try pinning certain buffers to reduce GC pauses.
[36:22] Maya: question — is pinning plat-specific? Like will pinning work on the cloud GPUs we use?
[36:30] Diego: it's platform dependent. On NVIDIA Ampere families pinning helps, on older hardware it may be less effective. We'll include hardware labels in the kernel matrix.
[36:45] Rajesh: our staging is on Ampere A10g, so pinning should be effective.
[36:52] Diego: good to know.
[37:10] Aisha: any blocker items that would prevent us from hitting the next milestone (pilot acceptance checkpoint)?
[37:20] Maya: main blocker is reproducing the microburst reliably, and getting a clean eval pass on q4 for long prompts. If those are ok we'll push to pilot acceptance.
[37:34] Aisha: ok we'll prioritize the reproducer and the quant sweep.
[37:44] [brief cross talk, someone's microphone pops, transcription rendered as 'mic pop']
[40:02] Diego: technical note I'll add to the repo: a patch to the kernel selector that forces 'fast-attn' for the first k layers for sequences between 256 and 768 to see if that avoids the memcpy cliff. It's experimental.
[40:20] Rajesh: we'll test in staging with A/B.
[40:28] Maya: if that works, what's the rollback plan?
[40:33] Diego: immediate rollback is to revert the config map and route all traffic back to the default kernel heuristic, that's immediate. We'll keep logs and a debug snapshot for 48 hours.
[40:45] Olivia: thanks, that sounds reasonable.
[41:00] Aisha: ok let's do a quick recap before we close. Decisions: 1) Disable hedging on streaming routes, 2) Run quant 4-bit vs 8-bit sweep (Diego), 3) Build and share microburst replay (Rajesh), 4) Provide kernel-selector toggle and config example (Diego), 5) Aisha to share microburst logs, audit snippets, and security checklist.
[41:28] Maya: and we'll confirm final success criteria by next Wednesday.
[41:34] Aisha: perfect. Any final questions?
[41:38] Olivia: none from me.
[41:40] Rajesh: none.
[41:42] Diego: all good.
[41:45] Aisha: thank you all. I'll follow up with notes, links, and the next meeting invite for the Friday deep debug if we reproduce the spike.
[41:55] Maya: thanks everyone.
[42:00] [meeting ends]
